data: Active Soyuz crewed pad — every ISS Soyuz crew rotation since 2020 has lifted from Site 31

Second active Soyuz pad at Baikonur Cosmodrome. R-7 era from 1961; modernised for Soyuz-2.1a in 2014. Took over the Soyuz crew programme from Site 1/5 in 2020. Every Soyuz MS crew rotation to the ISS since MS-16 has lifted from here. Coordinates from Roscosmos and FAI records.

The other half of the Baikonur Soyuz operation. Originally an R-7 ICBM pad from 1961; modernised for Soyuz-2.1a in 2014. When Site 1/5 went down for refurbishment in 2019, Site 31 picked up the entire Soyuz crew programme — every Soyuz MS rotation to the ISS since MS-16 in April 2020 has lifted from here. Continuous human spaceflight cadence: roughly two crews per year, with no interruption.
Sputnik 1 (1957). Vostok 1 — Gagarin (1961). Five hundred and forty Soyuz launches from a single pad.
Baikonur's Proton complex: Proton 1, Salyut 1, Mir and ISS modules, Mars and Luna probes
Russia's northern military cosmodrome — more launches than any other site
Plesetsk's workhorse Soyuz pad at 62.9°N — the world's highest-latitude active orbital launch complex
Proton pad — the Mir core, Salyut 7, Nauka, and probes from Venera to ExoMars
Russia's Soyuz-2 pad in the Far East: first launch 2016, OneWeb batches, Luna 25 (2023)
